data.title: Crypto Primary Investment: A Triangular Game Between Human Nature, Law, and Capital
data.description:
Author: IOSG Legal

Having worked in the crypto industry for many years, we've invested in hundreds of projects. Our understanding of investment terms in the industry has evolved from initial misunderstanding to acceptance, and now to reflection and skepticism:

When a project's structure becomes increasingly complex and its documentation increasingly technical, are we truly improving security, or merely making the risks appear more respectable? When agreements are filled with governance clauses, are these rights truly enforceable, or are they just empty words?

The systemic risks of Web3 investments often lie not in the market, but in the insufficient accountability of the architecture itself. Beautiful documentation and complete terminology, but in the worst-case scenario, investors cannot find the responsible party, cannot constrain control, and have no recourse—essentially, this is not risk control, but risk packaging.

Three recurring structural problems: I. Overly fragmented entities: Value, control, and responsibility are artificially separated. R&D/operations are in one company, token issuing and treasury are in another entity (foundation/SPV), and investors may only sign off on one of them. Superficially, it appears as risk isolation, but in reality, it's "risk without owner": when something goes wrong, everyone can say, "That wasn't me." What investors truly fear is never decentralization, but rather the loss of accountability. II. Symbolized governance: There are documents, but no mechanisms; there are rights, but no teeth. In the early days, investors made verbal promises and gentleman's agreements (which now seem like the adventurous spirit of a Western cowboy). Later, with SAFTE/SAFE/SAFT/SAFE+Token Warrants, key aspects remained missing: substantive consent for major matters, budgeting and auditing schedules for treasury expenditures, rules for replacing multi-signature signers, and the scope and boundaries of information disclosure. It reads like corporate governance, but in practice, it resembles a wish list. Third, the remedies are structurally weakened: Assets move faster than laws, entities change faster than procedures, and cross-border costs are higher than compensation—these are all reasons why it's difficult to protect one's rights in crypto investments. For investors, true risk control isn't about writing longer terms, but about ensuring that in the worst-case scenario, there's a way to "stop the bleeding," "seek redress," and "enforce the law." This industry has emerged from its early "dark forest" phase, but sudden project collapses remain commonplace. There are two root causes: first, some founders lack respect for the spirit of contracts; second, the industry lacks structural memory, with investors repeatedly making the same mistakes in structural design. This article discusses five real-world case scenarios, addressing structural problems that are often overlooked but can be fatal in extreme situations, distilling lessons learned into actionable principles. Case 1: From "Perfect Structure" to "Disappearing Defendant" [Keywords: Segmentation of Subject, Continued Legal Entity] Several years ago, we came across a project dedicated to building blockchain gaming infrastructure. The team had an impressive background and top-tier experience, and their "one-click on-chain" solution directly addressed the core pain points of traditional game developers. To raise funds and circumvent complex global regulations, the project designed a "perfect" offshore structure widely recognized at the time: registering a parent company in Delaware, USA, to handle technology development, while simultaneously establishing an SPV (Special Purpose Entity) in crypto-friendly Gibraltar specifically for issuing tokens. The technology and team were in the US, while the tokens resided in the offshore SPV—this was the prevailing consensus in the investment community at the time. Faced with this structure, investors typically take two paths: traditional equity investors invest in the parent company, reasoning that controlling the team means controlling the project. We chose a more "Crypto Native" path: directly signing a Token Purchase Agreement with the Gibraltar SPV, exchanging investment for future token rights. Our judgment was that since tokens are the core asset of this ecosystem's future, directly acquiring token rights is more direct than equity. At the time, this seemed like a fairly rational decision. After the investment, there was a relatively calm period. The project progressed slowly but steadily, and the team maintained polite and restrained communication with investors. However, one day, without notifying the US parent company or any investors, the Gibraltar SPV suddenly announced a change of CEO and almost simultaneously unilaterally launched a token issuance. The internal power struggle became public, market confidence collapsed instantly, and the price of the coin plummeted immediately upon listing. Our "coin rights" transformed overnight from potential value into highly volatile digital tokens. Our initial reaction was anger, but after calming down, we quickly assessed that this was more like a power struggle within the founding team. The SPV management was clearly trying to break free from the parent company's control, and the institutions that had invested in the parent company's equity would inevitably take legal action, potentially putting the project back on track. We chose to wait and see. Sure enough, the parent company and its equity investors quickly filed lawsuits in the US and Gibraltar, and initially succeeded: they successfully obtained a temporary restraining order from the US court, restoring the parent company's access to key technical infrastructure, and also obtained a freezing order from the Gibraltar court, freezing most of the tokens issued by the SPV. The parent company was likely to regain control. Then, an unexpected twist occurred. The Gibraltar court overturned the freeze order. The reason was chillingly simple: the US parent company had been administratively deregistered by the Delaware state government more than a year ago for failing to submit a single required compliance document for over a year. Legally, the company no longer existed. A company that was legally "dead" was not qualified to sue anyone. It had no legal personality, no legal capacity, and no interests that could be protected by the court. Those institutions that invested in the parent company's equity were completely ousted overnight. The legal entity they invested in had disappeared, and all their claims lost their foundation. Their investments were wiped out. Those of us who invested in SPV tokens, while our assets shrank dramatically due to the internal strife, at least still hold tradable tokens. Meanwhile, those equity investors who were once considered "safer" have completely lost their legal standing. More than relief, the feeling at that moment was one of lingering fear. The most fatal risk in this industry may not be a market crash, a technical vulnerability, or even the founder's character, but a forgotten compliance document that costs only a few hundred dollars. Case Conclusion The continuity of Legal Due Diligence (Legal DD) is crucial. The key to investment decisions lies not only in confirming the company's "good standing" status at the moment of signing the agreement, but also in establishing a continuous compliance monitoring mechanism throughout the entire investment cycle. Ensuring that every legal entity in the investment chain is "alive" and compliant is the most basic bottom line of investment management, yet it is often overlooked. A thorough understanding of the actual control of offshore structures is essential. When core assets (such as token issuance rights) are placed in an offshore SPV, and the parent company's control over the SPV relies solely on a single agreement, investors must be highly vigilant. Strong covenants must be included in the investment agreement, such as: the SPV's directors or controllers cannot be changed without the majority consent of the investors; the parent company must maintain its legal existence, otherwise default clauses will be triggered; any major decisions (such as token launches) must be approved by directors appointed by the investors. These clauses must be clearly stated at the outset of the investment, not be remedied after problems arise. Do not blindly trust lead investors. Even the top funds in the industry may have blind spots or undisclosed conflicts of interest in their due diligence. Independent, cross-validated background checks are indispensable. Investors must make their own independent judgments and be responsible for their own funds. Case Study 2: The "Evaporation" of Value – Entity Switching and Early Investor Dilution [Keywords: Entity Segmentation, Entity Switching and Dilution] There is another type of structural risk, more insidious, and often occurs within a "legal" framework. In 2021, amidst the market boom, we invested in a technology company specializing in formal verification. The team consisted of experts with top academic backgrounds, possessed strong technical capabilities, and consistently demonstrated great respect for investors, fostering a harmonious working relationship. However, about two or three years later, we gradually discovered that the founders began to build a completely new token issuance entity, intending to advance the token project under an entity entirely separate from the original investment company. Even more unacceptable was that this new entity neither gave any recognition to the early equity investors nor attempted to include them in the new token equity framework. From a legal perspective, their actions were technically flawless: the new entity was independently registered, and the original investment contracts did not directly bind the new entity's behavior. But from a business perspective, this was a systemic deprivation of the value of early investors—the early investors nurtured a team and a set of technologies with their funds and trust, only to have these resources "re-germinate" within the new entity, while the original equity structure was quietly hollowed out. We then represented all early investors in months of difficult negotiations with the founders, arguing our case and insisting on securing their due rights. Ultimately, we obtained more favorable valuation terms for the early investors than for the new round of investors. However, this process nearly exhausted our established relationships with the founders. This experience made us realize that entity switching can be the most "elegant" way to plunder value. Case Conclusion: Include an "entity switching protection clause" in the investment agreement. Clearly stipulate that if the founders establish a new affiliated entity and promote the issuance of core assets (especially tokens) within a certain period after the investment (ideally 2-3 years), early investors should receive a corresponding equity share. This clause should be included in the agreement at the time of the initial investment, rather than being remedied after problems arise. Governance rights are more important than valuation. Board seats and the right to know and consent to major structural changes are the last line of defense for protecting the interests of early investors. Relationships and trust alone are not enough. Case Study 3: When Human Nature Becomes a Variable—Bailout Financing and Failed Promises [Keywords in this case: Structurally weakened relief pathways] If the first two cases were cold games of law and structure, this case is full of entanglements of human feelings and human nature. Sometimes, what defeats you is not complex terms, but a face that changes rapidly in the face of self-interest. It was during the deepest part of the bear market that an early investment project of ours was running out of funds and on the verge of bankruptcy. The founder pleaded that there was no money left in the account and that without new funding, it would be impossible to continue operations. Out of concern for protecting existing investments and a glimmer of hope for the project, we decided to extend a helping hand and conduct a down-round rescue funding round at a lower valuation. The founder was deeply grateful at the time. With the funds in place, the project was able to survive. The market soon recovered, and the sector the project was in became a hot topic. The founder, thanks to this "lifeline," weathered the storm and, coupled with excellent storytelling skills, ultimately secured a new round of follow-on investment from well-known institutions and successfully listed on major exchanges. However, communication with the founder subsequently became extremely difficult. When investors wanted them to fulfill their initial promises, they began a series of excuses—from initially refusing to distribute tokens to investors through a Coinbase listing, to using various reasons such as illness of themselves or family members to delay—the entire process lasted for months. The final showdown: either accept the same terms as other new investors, or give up. The initial act of helping was disregarded in the face of enormous profits. Fortunately, our legal and post-investment teams never gave up. Through long-term, patient communication and rights protection, we ultimately recovered the vast majority of the tokens we were owed. But this experience revealed a fundamental problem: changes in the distribution of benefits can systematically alter human behavior. This is not a pessimistic view of human nature, but a variable that should be designed into the contract structure in advance. Case Conclusion Do not relax your requirements for legal documents simply because the other party is humble. Business decisions should always be based on worst-case scenarios. Rescue financing during a bear market often occurs when information asymmetry is greatest and emotional pressure is highest—precisely when legal requirements are most easily relaxed. The more humble the other party's stance and the greater your negotiating advantage, the more you must insist on including all commitments in the formal agreement. Given the scarcity of contractual integrity, you must ensure the agreement's execution through clauses with "teeth." Investment agreements must clearly define penalties for breach of contract. For example, if the other party fails to fulfill specific terms, it should trigger hefty penalties or grant investors the right to acquire more tokens at extremely low prices. The cost of breach should significantly outweigh the potential gains from such breach. Simultaneously, ensure investors have sufficient negotiating leverage, such as board seats, veto power over major decisions, or joint control over the company's bank accounts and multi-signature wallets. Before deciding to provide assistance, let's answer a fundamental question: What is the root cause of this team's financial crisis? Can their values ​​withstand stress tests? Adhering to transparency and compliance is not a lack of trust in the founders, but rather the most basic protection of the relationship between the two parties. Case 4: Governance Failure – The Cost of Silence [Keywords in this case: Symbolized Governance] There is a type of risk that is neither a loophole in the legal structure nor a subjective betrayal by the founders, but rather the absence of investors at crucial moments. We once invested in a promising Web3 infrastructure project. Behind the project was a highly respected and wealthy major shareholder, which was one of the key reasons we were optimistic about it. However, at an all-staff meeting, this major shareholder publicly dismissed the CEO, catching the entire team completely off guard. We only learned of this afterward from the departing CEO, not from an official announcement from the project team. Our initial assessment was that this was merely a normal management adjustment and did not constitute a crisis signal requiring immediate intervention. We did not request an audit, did not request a special shareholders' meeting, and did not initiate any evaluation procedures; we chose silence and observation. Approximately six months to a year later, the new management announced that the foundation would be liquidated. We ultimately only recovered less than 20% of our initial investment. In retrospect, the CEO's sudden dismissal was the clearest warning sign of the project's decline. When a company experiences significant and unusual management changes, it often indicates deep cracks in its core governance structure. At that time, the most important thing investors should do is immediately demand an independent audit and intervene in governance reconstruction, rather than standing idly by. Case Conclusion: Major governance events should be designated as mandatory "intervention trigger events." The investment agreement should clearly state that significant events such as the CEO's unexcused departure, changes in core shareholders, or the initiation of litigation or arbitration will automatically trigger the investor's special rights, including demanding an independent financial audit, convening a special shareholders' meeting, and suspending significant financial expenditures. Continuous monitoring, rather than passive waiting, is crucial. Post-investment management should not stop at routine quarterly updates. Investors need to establish proactive information acquisition channels, including maintaining communication with the project's core employees (not just the founders). It is recommended that the post-investment agreement require the project to provide independent updates at the CFO/CTO level every quarter, rather than relying solely on the founders. Case Study 5: The Halo of a Resume—A Black Hole of Character [Key words in this case: Governance is symbolized, and relief pathways are structurally weakened] It's often said in the investment world, "Investing is about investing in people." However, we are too easily misled by a glittering resume. Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, top hedge funds… these names seem to have an inherent halo, subconsciously equating "elite background" with "professionalism, self-discipline, and reliability." But the harsh reality is that sometimes, the most dangerous are precisely these "golden boys." Wall Street training teaches them to package narratives, exploit rules, and manipulate people's hearts. These abilities are neither good nor bad in themselves, but once misused, their destructive power far exceeds imagination. We once "luckily" missed out on a project. The founder's resume was impeccable, rising through the ranks from Goldman Sachs to JPMorgan Chase before starting his own business. His project was an "absolutely fair" on-chain casino. The story was captivating, the team impressive, and numerous well-known institutions in the industry were vying for entry. However, due to our significant concerns about the compliance risks of the "casino" sector, after multiple unsuccessful attempts to discuss compliance pathways with the founder, our risk control department ultimately rejected the investment. The turning point came the day after we made our decision. The project announced the completion of a multi-million dollar funding round. However, within minutes of the funds arriving, the founder began transferring company money into his personal wallet. Over the next week, he gambled away millions of dollars in another on-chain casino app. He promised to build a fair casino, but instead used the money to build a casino to gamble in someone else's establishment. This wasn't a failure of risk management; it was blatant fraud and misappropriation. Ultimately, the FBI intervened, the founder was arrested, and faces years in prison. Another case we witnessed firsthand involved a AAA game hailed as the "Call of Duty on the blockchain." The team members all came from top game studios, but the project burned through cash at an alarming rate, reaching two to three million US dollars per month, while development was severely delayed. The company quickly fell into a financial crisis, and the team dwindled from over a hundred people to just over a dozen. Just as this empire was crumbling, we discovered that the project's co-founder and CTO had been continuously selling his own team tokens on the secondary market for seven months, accumulating nearly 700,000 US dollars in cash. Legally, he was selling his own vested shares, which seemed perfectly acceptable. From a business ethics perspective, with the company on the brink of collapse and numerous employees laid off, one of the core leaders was frantically cashing out personally. The message to the market couldn't be clearer: "The ship is sinking, I'm jumping first." In both cases, investors focused excessively on the founders' past achievements, neglecting a thorough examination of their current character and behavioral patterns. Furthermore, the lack of crucial control over "multiple signatures" and "milestone payments" was the direct cause of the loss of control over funds. Case Conclusion: Character Due Diligence (DD) must be paramount. Resumes can be embellished, stories can be packaged, but a person's character and behavioral patterns are relatively stable. Investment institutions need to establish a more systematic due diligence methodology, going beyond routine background checks to potentially include more in-depth interviews and even behavioral stress tests. Of particular concern is whether there is a fundamental contradiction between the founder's personal history and the project's stated mission. A person with a gambling history running a casino is a huge red flag. Fund control is a non-negotiable bottom line in investment. For early-stage projects, especially those where the founder holds a dominant position, all funds should never be placed in a wallet completely controlled by the founder. Multi-signature wallets should be mandatory, and investors or their designated, trusted third parties must be among the multi-signature participants. Fund releases should be based on clear, quantifiable milestones—completing one task before releasing the next. These risk control measures, already mature in the traditional VC industry, should be strictly enforced in the crypto industry. Deeply align the core team's interests with the project's long-term development. The unlocking of team tokens should not only be linked to time, but also to project milestones, such as product launch, reaching a certain user base, or achieving a certain level of protocol revenue. Simultaneously, the agreement should clearly stipulate that the sale of tokens by core members will be restricted during periods of financial distress or major crisis. This is both a constraint and a gesture, demonstrating to the community and all investors the team's determination to stand with the project through thick and thin. Conclusion: Returning to Common Sense, Navigating Cycles Having experienced so much, we are no longer the passionate "Web3 believers." We have become more like realists, risk assessors, and observers of human nature. We no longer get easily excited by grand narratives; instead, we examine every detail like auditors and test every hypothesis like engineers. When evaluating a project, we now repeatedly ask ourselves: Do we really understand this founder? Besides his own story, have we learned about him indirectly, from his former colleagues, former bosses, or even competitors? Do we truly understand the legal structure of this project? Are there any hidden "backdoors"? If the founder absconds, will the contracts we hold be worthless or a powerful weapon? After the funding is injected, do we have control over how the funds are used? Or can we only pin our hopes on the founders' moral conscience? Are the interests of the founding team truly aligned with those of us investors? Does their token unlocking mechanism encourage long-term development or facilitate short-term cash-outs? When we discover signs of problems, do we have the courage to say no? Ultimately, a good investment structure isn't about protecting against honest people, but against extreme situations. When everyone is respectable, any structure functions well; the real test is whether your contracts can speak for you in times of conflicting interests, market upheavals, and collapsing trust. We learned these lessons with real money. We wrote these down because we believe that the cost of industry progress should not be repeatedly paid by each new generation of entrants. This is why we have systematically introduced mechanisms such as continuous compliance monitoring, entity switching protection clauses, and mandatory multi-signature wallet requirements into our investment process. These are not just improvements on paper, but rather institutional upgrades that have been refined through repeated real-world cost-cutting.

data.title: Java4Shell: Critical Java Vulnerability Puts Enterprise Systems at Risk
data.description:
A Critical Vulnerability in Java

A newly disclosed vulnerability known as Java4Shell has triggered cybersecurity warnings worldwide, raising concerns about organisations that rely on Java-powered applications and enterprise infrastructure.

Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw affects OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, a component commonly used to process encoded data. Researchers found that specially crafted input could trigger memory corruption, potentially allowing attackers to expose sensitive information, crash applications or execute malicious code remotely.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning because Java is deeply embedded in enterprise environments, powering authentication systems, software development pipelines, internal business applications and critical infrastructure.

How Java4Shell Works

The flaw exists within a hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding function used by OpenJDK on certain supported x86-64 processors. Under specific conditions, malformed input can cause the decoder to write beyond its allocated memory boundaries, corrupting neighbouring memory.

Depending on the application and exploit conditions, this could potentially allow attackers to:

  • Read sensitive information from memory, including tokens, credentials or other secrets.
  • Crash Java processes, disrupting business applications and services.
  • Execute arbitrary code remotely, potentially gaining control over affected servers.

Researchers demonstrated exploit scenarios involving widely used enterprise applications, including Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate.

Some demonstrations achieved remote code execution without authentication under tested configurations. However, exploitation is not universal and depends on the affected Java runtime, hardware capabilities and how an application processes attacker-controlled input.

AI Accelerated Vulnerability Discovery

One of the most notable aspects of Java4Shell is the reported role of artificial intelligence in discovering and exploiting the flaw.

Security researchers at Calif reportedly used AI-assisted analysis to identify the vulnerability in approximately one hour and developed an initial working exploit within another two hours, at a reported cost of less than US$200 in AI usage.

The discovery highlights how AI tools can assist researchers in analysing complex codebases, identifying weaknesses in low-level software components and accelerating exploit development.

While human expertise was still required to guide and validate the process, the speed demonstrates how AI may lower the time, cost and technical barriers associated with vulnerability research.

This also raises concerns that threat actors could use similar tools to identify weaknesses and develop targeted exploits more rapidly.

Why Enterprises Face Greater Exposure

Java4Shell poses a particular challenge to enterprises because Java environments are often distributed across large and complex IT infrastructures.

Organisations may operate multiple Java versions across servers, containers, cloud workloads and third-party applications. Some installations may be embedded within software packages, making them less visible to traditional asset inventories.

Applications such as identity management platforms, CI/CD pipelines, internal collaboration tools and software repositories are especially sensitive. A successful compromise could potentially expose credentials, source code, internal documentation or privileged access mechanisms, enabling attackers to move deeper into an organisation's network.

The vulnerability also has specific hardware requirements, meaning not every Java system is affected equally. Nevertheless, identifying every vulnerable runtime and confirming whether the required processor capabilities are present can be a significant operational challenge.

Patching and Mitigation Priorities

Oracle released security updates addressing Java4Shell on 17 November, while cybersecurity agencies urged organisations to identify affected systems and apply vendor patches promptly.

Organisations should prioritise:

  • Java asset discovery: Identify all Java installations, including runtimes bundled within third-party applications and containers.
  • Immediate patching: Update affected Java distributions and verify that running services are using the patched versions.
  • Exposure reduction: Restrict public access to vulnerable applications, particularly identity, development and administrative systems.
  • Monitoring: Review logs for suspicious requests, unusual application behaviour, crashes and potential exploitation attempts.
  • Incident readiness: Assess whether exposed systems may have suffered memory disclosure, credential compromise or unauthorised execution.

Organisations unable to patch immediately should consult their Java and application vendors for temporary mitigation guidance and consider reducing exposure until updates can be deployed.

Conclusion: AI Is Accelerating Both Discovery and Risk

Java4Shell illustrates the growing cybersecurity implications of AI-assisted vulnerability research. Tools that help security professionals identify flaws faster can also reduce the time available for organisations to respond before attackers attempt exploitation.

The vulnerability further demonstrates that widely trusted software foundations are not immune to security weaknesses, even when applications are built on mature programming platforms.

As AI continues to accelerate security research and exploit development, organisations will need stronger software inventory management, faster patching processes and more proactive vulnerability assessment to keep pace with an increasingly compressed threat landscape.

Sources:

  • Newsweek — How Java4Shell Cybersecurity Bug Threatens Organizations, Experts, November 2026.
  • Reuters — German cyber security agency warns of critical Java4Shell vulnerability, 18 November 2026.
  • Reuters — Governments warn Java flaw leaves computer systems open to hackers, November 2026.
  • BleepingComputer — Critical Java4Shell flaw allows RCE attacks on major Java applications, 17 November 2026.
  • The Record / Recorded Future News — CISA warns of Java4Shell, an AI-found Java bug touching most of the Fortune 500, 18 November 2026.

data.title: From "King of Trading" to Nearly 10 Billion Yuan in Unrealized Losses: Tom Lee and the Valuation Dilemma of Ethereum
data.description:
Author: Zhou, ChainCatcher

For E-guards, the past year has been exceptionally difficult.

Since reaching an all-time high of $4,954 last year, the price of ETH has been declining steadily. This year, ETH has repeatedly fallen below the $2,000 mark, even dipping below $1,600 in June, and is currently hovering around $1,800, a pullback of over 60% from its all-time high.

Author: Zhou, ChainCatcher

The most severely affected company is Bitmine, led by Tom Lee. As of November 8th, the company held 6,070,092 ETH, with an average cost of approximately $3,353, resulting in unrealized losses that once approached 10 billion US dollars.

More than a year ago, this co-founder of Fundstrat, as a Wall Street strategist, endorsed ETH and was considered a rare institutional spokesperson for Ethereum.

Regardless of market conditions afterward, he almost always found reasons to be bullish. At the end of October this year, he still stated that ETH was expected to reach approximately $62,000 in the next cycle. From the market's perspective, his statements increasingly resembled "brainless bullishness." How much is the value of the words of a bull who has nearly halved his holdings and is experiencing unrealized losses of nearly 10 billion? I. Why is Tom Lee no longer able to promote ETH? The second half of last year was when Tom Lee's influence was at its peak. Bitmine, leveraging its share price premium, continuously issued new tokens to buy more coins, becoming the world's largest ETH treasury company in just a few months. Tom Lee's several short-term predictions also came true, earning him the title of "ETH trading king." Even after ETH peaked and fell back in August, his bullish stance remained unchanged. At Binance Blockchain Week in early December, he still claimed that ETH at $3,000 was severely undervalued and predicted that both BTC and ETH would reach new highs in January 2026. Two weeks later, an internal report shattered this image. On December 20th, Sean Farrell, Head of Digital Asset Strategy at Fundstrat, in his 2026 outlook for paid subscribers, used a significant pullback in the first half of the year as a baseline scenario, giving a target range of $1,800 to $2,000 for ETH and $60,000 to $65,000 for BTC. From "King of Trading" to Nearly 10 Billion Yuan in Unrealized Losses: Tom Lee and the Valuation Dilemma of ETH" The contrast between publicly advocating for a bullish stance and internally expressing a bearish view has plunged Tom Lee and his team into a crisis of trust, with many seeing it as the beginning of Tom Lee's image collapse. Sean Farrell later clarified that the report emphasized risk management and did not represent a bearish outlook. Tom Lee explained that the two stemmed from different methodologies and timeframes. Subsequent market movements largely aligned with the predictions of that internal report. In January 2026, neither BTC nor ETH reached new highs. ETH subsequently fell below $2,000 multiple times, even dropping below $1,600 in June. Since September 2025, he had repeatedly suggested that ETH could reach approximately $62,000. According to his calculations, if Ethereum replaced payment and banking infrastructure, the ETH/BTC exchange rate could rise to approximately 0.25. Based on BTC's $250,000 valuation, ETH would be around $62,000. He later added historical cycle evidence, stating that Ethereum had previously increased 50 to 200 times, and even a conservative estimate of 25 times would reach this price level. Regarding the decline in ETH, in Bitmine's weekly report on November 16th, he described the 28% drop in ETH within two weeks as a waterfall-like decline inconsistent with fundamentals, possibly due to external factors such as Nvidia's developments and investors raising cash for Anthropic's IPO. A year ago, his reason was the damage to market makers' balance sheets. Beyond credibility, Bitmine's own situation is also weakening Tom Lee's influence. The model of issuing new tokens to buy coins that supported its expansion last year is now unsustainable. As ETH prices fell, Bitmine's stock price remained below the value of its holdings for an extended period. Continuing to issue new shares would only dilute shareholders, so Bitmine turned to share buybacks. According to Bitmine's disclosure, as of late October 2026, the company had repurchased approximately 22.9 million shares, costing about $400 million. In the past two weeks, Bitmine purchased 9,587 and 7,653 ETH respectively, the latter worth approximately $14 million at current prices, indicating a significant reduction in the scale of its acquisitions. The company has now achieved 99% of its 5% holding target and has not yet disclosed its plans after reaching that target, making it highly likely that it will not purchase any more ETH. More importantly, Bitmine's scarcity as a bridge between Wall Street and ETH is diminishing. In January of this year, Grayscale completed the first distribution of staking yield for a spot ETH ETF in the US. In March, BlackRock launched a staking-based ETH ETF, allowing institutions to directly obtain ETH exposure and staking yields through the ETF. Currently, Bitmine has virtually no debt, with approximately 86% of its ETH pledged, generating an annualized staking income of about $245 million. There is no pressure for forced liquidation in the short term. While Tom Lee's public image hasn't completely collapsed, his words have a significantly less impact on the market than before. II. After the ETH burning narrative fails, can value storage still convince the public? A review of Tom Lee's bullish logic over the past year reveals that the most frequently mentioned aspect is the tokenization supercycle. In his view, tokenization is making steady progress, mostly on Ethereum. From a usage perspective, tokenization is indeed happening. According to a Binance Research report, Ethereum network usage grew by approximately 50% in the first half of 2026, but due to continuously declining gas fees, full-year network revenue is projected to decrease by 53%. The chain is becoming increasingly busy, but value hasn't returned to ETH. Since the shift to proof-of-stake, ETH has fallen by more than 60% relative to BTC. The burning logic that previously supported ETH's valuation has also become ineffective. With the advancement of L2 scaling and a significant decrease in mainnet fees, the amount burned is far from keeping up with the new issuance. According to data from ultrasound.money, based on the most recent 30 days, the annualized burn of ETH is approximately 35,000 coins, the annualized issuance is approximately 1.09 million coins, and the annual supply growth rate is approximately 0.86%. Since the merger, the net increase in ETH supply is approximately 1.7 million coins, completely dashing deflationary expectations. Bitcoin's position as digital gold largely stems from its minimal rule changes over the years, while Ethereum continues its rapid iteration. On November 8th, Vitalik Buterin reiterated ETH's value store positioning and stated that he would no longer use transaction fee burning as a core valuation logic. In his view, past burning primarily stemmed from speculative demand within the crypto community and did not represent a true price bottom. Pursuing high burning amounts would conflict with the goals of decentralization and anti-capture. Even if burning consistently falls below 10% of the break-even level, there's no need to regret it. Tom Lee, as always, included Vitalik's affirmation of ETH as a value store in his bullish analysis. Institutional investors, however, hold a different view. According to Jeff Dorman, Chief Investment Officer of Arca, Ethereum's monthly revenue of approximately $6 million, plus the ETH held in wallets for gas payments, can only explain $45 billion to $50 billion of its approximately $246 billion market capitalization. The remainder comes from social value and market imagination. Crypto KOL Blue Fox also believes that it's too early to talk about value storage. Ethereum should first charge a reasonable fee of 10% to 20% from L2 and block builders to fundamentally solve the value capture problem. Value storage can only form naturally; it cannot be achieved by simply shouting slogans. Vitalik Buterin mentioned that Ethereum's roadmap is relatively mature, and most major changes can be predicted in advance. However, he also listed a long list of protocol features that are expected to change, including a significant adjustment to the consensus algorithm within the next two years. Crypto KOL Chen Mo stated that the impact of technological routes on prices takes a long time to materialize. What truly matters is whether Ethereum can continue to attract developers; data destruction is secondary. Thirdly, with the foundation stepping back, can Bitmine take over? Ethereum may be very successful, but why ETH must be so expensive remains a question without a convincing answer. In his long post on X, Vitalik wrote that if holding ETH is about chasing financial trends, then a fearless leader shouting slogans on social media is needed. This statement carries a hint of irony and indicates that the foundation has no intention of playing such a role.

The foundation's mission document, released in March of this year, listed resistance to censorship and capture as core principles.

Meanwhile, the foundation is experiencing internal turmoil. Two co-executive directors, Tomasz Stańczak and Hsiao-Wei Wang, resigned in February and June respectively, and are currently being temporarily managed by board member Bastian Aue. In June, the foundation announced layoffs of 54 people, approximately 20% of its total staff, and a reduction of about 40% in its annual budget.

Recently, Kayleen Fulton, former head of protocol support for the foundation, filed a lawsuit in U.S. federal court alleging that she and Trent Van Epps spearheaded a 53-signature open letter opposing controversial clauses in the mission statement. Both were subsequently dismissed in April. The foundation has not yet filed a response. Furthermore, there have been frequent reports in the market recently that the foundation is selling off ETH, with multiple wallets marked as being associated with the foundation selling ETH. According to on-chain analyst Ai Yi, since October 26, addresses associated with the foundation have sold approximately 7,785 ETH. However, on-chain analyst Specter cautions that the ownership of some wallets lacks sufficient evidence, and while there may have been early financial dealings with the foundation, this does not necessarily mean that the foundation still controls them. From a scale perspective, these sales have a limited direct impact on price. The foundation holds approximately 0.16% of the total ETH supply and has pledged about 70,000 ETH this year, using the proceeds to offset some of the sales. However, from the perspective of retail investors, Vitalik's positioning of ETH as a store of value, coupled with the continuous news of the foundation selling tokens, is shaking market confidence. It is worth noting that the buyers in the foundation's publicly confirmed sales are all Bitmine. According to the foundation's announcements, from March to May, the foundation sold a total of 25,000 ETH to Bitmine through three over-the-counter transactions, with an average transaction price between $2,043 and $2,387. In June of this year, five former senior researchers at the foundation founded Ethlabs, a non-profit research and development organization, with funders including BitMine, SharpLink, and Ethereum co-founder Joe Lubin. In July, the same group of funders supported the establishment of Ethereum Institutional, a company focused on institutional promotion and ETH marketing. However, the connection between the two is currently limited to buying, selling, and funding. After Vitalik reiterated his concept of a store of value, for this argument to be accepted by Wall Street, it needs to be translated into a valuation logic that institutions can understand. Finally, for ETH investors, there are very few entities left to rely on. The foundation has no intention of advocating for the price of the coin, and funds in spot ETFs have been flowing out recently. Bitmine, holding approximately 5% of the circulating ETH supply, is still considered the most motivated and capable party to support the ETH narrative. The problem is that Bitmine's interests don't entirely overlap with those of retail investors. Its revenue primarily comes from staking, its stock price performance depends on asset premiums, and its acquisition scale has significantly decreased after approaching the 5% target. Tom Lee's hawkish pronouncements are no longer likely to sway the market. Rather than focusing on his next target price, it might be more worthwhile to see if Bitmine can establish a more direct collaboration with its foundation to find a valuation anchor for ETH that is recognized by Wall Street.

data.title: Grayscale: Did Anthropic surge after its IPO? Traders bet on Hyperliquid.
data.description:
Authors: Zach Pandl, Head of Research at Grayscale; Michael Zhao, Senior Researcher; Translator: Shaw, Jinse Finance

Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq on November 19, but traders have been playing the price action on the on-chain trading platform Hyperliquid for weeks. If traders are right, Anthropic's opening price could be about 23% higher than the bid price range.

How does Hyperliquid achieve this kind of price discovery?

... Traders use pre-IPO perpetual contracts, cash-settled contracts used to track the potential trading price of the underlying stock; the contracts themselves do not carry any equity ownership. Since Anthropic has not yet established a public stock price, individual deployers build their own reference prices, known as "oracles." Trade.xyz is the largest third-party deployer on Hyperliquid in terms of trading volume and open interest: it sets its own initial contract price, which is then determined by market dynamics, essentially allowing the market to provide its own expectations. Entropy, the second largest third-party deployer, combines its own trading data with private market price data for pricing; during periods of high trading activity, it relies more heavily on its own market data. Both platforms' contracts will switch to being pegged to the Nasdaq's real-time price after the underlying stock is officially listed. The recent trading price of Trade.xyz's contract tracking Anthropic Class A common stock is approximately $96, significantly higher than the $70–$78 trading range (Chart 1). While the historical record of this type of market is short, it is valuable for reference. In the previous 8 IPO cases, this market accurately predicted the opening price of the new stock to be higher or lower than the issue price 7 times. The only misjudgment was the Hong Kong listing of SHEIN: at that time, the contract price was about 9% lower than the issue price, while the stock opened at the issue price, but fell by 10% within an hour of opening. For investors, the core conclusion is not that this type of contract can accurately predict the opening price, but that it can provide all-weather, real-time signals of capital demand before a company goes public, which is something that traditional markets cannot provide. This Thursday's opening will be another test of this signal. Key Points: Anthropic is expected to complete its IPO on November 19 (Thursday). Traders on the on-chain platform Hyperliquid can now express their bullish or bearish views or hedge risks 24/7 through pre-IPO perpetual contracts. data.title: The consensus among Fed hawks is heating up, with two figures advocating for a move of over 25 basis points in December.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

Support for further tightening of monetary policy within the Federal Reserve is increasing. The minutes of the October 27-28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, released Wednesday, show that **almost all participating officials believed that interest rates may still need to be raised in the coming months** to ensure that inflation falls back to the 2% target level in a timely manner.

The minutes stated, "In the coming months, almost all participants believed that, based on their baseline forecasts of inflation and the labor market, it may be necessary to further raise the target range for the federal funds rate to ensure that inflation returns to the 2% target level in a timely manner."

Among them, **two policymakers proposed a more aggressive rate hike plan. They believed that if subsequent inflation data performed poorly, the December rate hike might need to be "more than 25 basis points."

This reflects broad support within the Federal Reserve for further interest rate hikes, but the specific magnitude and pace of these increases remain points of contention among policymakers. The Federal Reserve's October meeting decided to maintain interest rates unchanged by a 10-2 vote. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted against a 25-basis-point hike. Previously, the Fed had raised rates by 25 basis points in September, its first rate hike in three years. The meeting minutes also revealed that several officials who supported keeping rates unchanged in October believed the decision "almost changed." However, other officials in the majority believe that market expectations for further rate hikes in December and 2027 are "broadly consistent" with their assessment of the appropriate monetary policy. They believe these expectations also reduce the risks associated with the Fed's decision not to raise rates in October. The disagreement extends beyond whether rates should be raised; it also concerns how the Fed should communicate its future policy direction to the market. The meeting minutes show that some officials who supported an October rate hike appeared dissatisfied with the Fed's previous policy communication methods. They stated that they might have supported maintaining the current interest rate, but only if market participants clearly understood that further tightening of monetary policy was likely in the future. The disagreement among officials focuses on the magnitude of rate hikes and policy signals. Comments made earlier on Wednesday by Fed Governor Christopher Waller also indicate that some officials support accelerating policy tightening. In an interview with CNBC, Waller stated that he supports a 50-basis-point rate hike by the Federal Reserve in December. He later added that if this 50-basis-point increase were to be implemented in two phases, in December and January, policymakers would need to send a "credible signal" to the market that another rate hike would occur in January. However, other officials do not share the same view on the pace of rate hikes. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly stated on Wednesday that the Fed should take a cautious and prudent approach when raising rates. Fed Governor Michael Barr also stated that further rate increases might be appropriate. In contrast, New York Fed President John Williams on Tuesday dismissed the idea that the Fed needs to consider a large rate hike. Interest rate futures currently reflect investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by 25 basis points each in December and January, followed by another rate hike in April. This market pricing indicates that investors have already priced in continued rate hikes over the next few months, but policymakers still have differing opinions on the magnitude and timing of each hike. Inflationary pressures and a weak housing market create a policy tug-of-war. Inflation data further strengthens the case for rate hikes. October consumer price data shows that price increases have spread to more everyday consumer goods and services. A portion of wholesale prices is included in the Fed's preferred inflation measure, and these prices saw their fastest year-over-year increase since 2022 in October. However, continued interest rate hikes could have a greater impact on some sectors of the economy that are highly dependent on borrowing, including the housing market. Data released this week highlights the weakness in the US housing market. Last month, existing home sales fell to their lowest level in 16 years. Sluggish housing activity is also a reason for some officials to advocate for a cautious approach to interest rate hikes. When the Federal Reserve makes its interest rate decision in October, the US midterm elections are also in their final days. However, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh previously told reporters that he did not hear any discussion about the elections during the interest rate decision meeting. AI investment becomes a new risk variable. Federal Reserve officials' concerns about inflation have expanded from factors such as energy and tariffs to more areas of the economy. The meeting minutes show that officials generally agreed that "inflationary pressures in the economy are widespread," thus necessitating further action. AI investment was also listed as one of the core topics of discussion. Policymakers noted that AI-related demand "will pose a significant inflation risk." The Fed staff briefing officials also warned that complex financing arrangements between AI companies could amplify industry risks, including off-balance-sheet lease commitments and revolving financing structures. These arrangements could further amplify losses should related investments fall short of expectations. The minutes stated: "Most participants noted that AI-related debt is growing rapidly, and a significant portion of this growth comes from complex and opaque financing structures. A few participants noted that AI-related risk exposure is increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few companies." This means that the Fed's focus on the AI ​​boom is no longer limited to inflationary pressures from infrastructure investment, but also includes issues such as corporate debt growth, financing transparency, and the concentration of financial risks. However, officials still expect inflation to fall sharply in 2027 and beyond as the effects of the current shock gradually subside.
